description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
**Output 1 in the proposal: 20 Palestinian water professionals (at least 30% female) have increased knowledge on best practices in inclusive water governance and water cycle management**
This output was completely achieved as 20 participants attended and completed the NL training, where the focus was on water governance and water cycle management. These participants all received a certificate of completion. However the percentage of female participants was 20% rather than 30%.
**Output 2 in the proposal: 20 Palestinian water professionals (at least 30% female) have the capacity to develop, implement and evaluate trainings aimed at adult colleagues or stakeholders in participatory water governance and effective wastewater management**
This output was completely achieved as 22 participants attended and completed the online, which included an entire training-of-trainers component. However the percentage of female participants was 20% rather than 30%. Only 16 of the 22 participants ended up attending the NL training, which means that 6 participants from the online training did not continue their learning and thus are not considered as graduates. However they still obtained important information on how to be an effective trainer in their own context.
In total, 26 water professionals took part in at least one of the different training activities of this project.
Furthermore, there will be a total of 3 training plans developed as an output from this training (compared with 1 training plan in the proposal). One of the training plans is already completed and submiited, and the two remaining training plans are being finalised and will be sent shortly).
**Output 3 in the proposal: 20 Palestinian water professionals (at least 30% female) have developed Back Home Action Plans for integrating gained knowledge and skills into their own context**
This output was completely achieved however in a slightly different manner. Instead of having the participants prepare 20 individual Back Home Action Plans, the decision was made by the facilitators and requesting organisations to encourage participants to work together in groups. This enhances the quality of the plans because it allows for sharing of ideas, division of responsibilities and tasks, and a better chance of future implementation when multiple people are involved. Therefore all participants were involved in developing Back Home Action Plans and training plans, however the number of outputs was less than 20 because everyone worked in teams. There will be a total of 6 Back Home Action Plans (all have been submitted however some are being updated based on facilitator's comments).
No progress on outputs. All training activities were postponed to 2021.

- 20 mid and senior staff members (minimum 6 women)

15-11-2022: The TMT consisted of two main training activities: • A first online training from 20 June - 16 July, 2021 • A second face-to-face training in the Netherlands from 8 - 12 November, 2021
The online training had a total of 22 participants, all of whom completed the training. From this group, 16 participants were selected to attend the NL training alongside 4 additional participants (for a total of 20 participants). All of these 20 participants completed the NL training and received a certificate of completion.
All together 26 participants where involved in at least one training component within this TMT.

comment.narrative: Female participants can actively engage in training discussions and presentations
01-09-2022: All training activities were postponed to 2021

15-11-2022: The Hague Academy prepared a participant profile to help Palestinian Water Authority (PWA) select candidates for the training. In the participant profile, it was mentioned that a minimum of 30% of participants should be female (preferably 40%). During the NL training, women participants were placed in the same hotel rooms so they would not have to share a room with a male colleague. During the NL training session was delivered on "participation and inclusion in water management" with a focus on gender inclusion. During the NL and online trainings, female participants were encouraged by facilitators and the experts to speak up and share their opinions in plenary. Women participants were involved in all group discussions and final presentations.

2 municipalities to receive training from alumni

28-11-2022: A total of 3 requesting (beneficiary) organisations in the Palestinian Territories were strengthened by the group training (PWA, Salfeet Municipality, North Hebron Joint Service Council). Based on the results of the evaluation survey and discussions, the training met their needs, provided new knowledge and skills, and improved governance of their operations.
The two implementing organisations (The Hague Academy, World Waternet) were also strengthened the group training. The Hague Academy became more familiar with the Palestinian context, developed new training materials that can be used in other trainings, organised new study visits in partnership with World Waternet experts, and implemented a training in Amsterdam for the first time. World Waterned benefited from hosting a training on its premises and allowing its staff to interact with the participants, and from observing the training methodology from The Hague Academy which they would like to use in future internal and external capacity building. This training was also directly beneficial to World Waternet's Blue Deal programme activities by building the capacity of the 3 local requesting organisations to implement projects and work alongside Dutch partners.
